chapters.name: Chapter 1: How a solar home system works

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The parts of a solar home system, and quality
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Name the parts of a solar home system and check whether a kit is certified.
This lesson builds toward: Given a solar home system kit, you will name each part (panel, charge controller, battery, inverter, lights and appliances) and check whether the kit is certified in the VeraSol database, naming all the parts correctly and recording the certification result.
A solar home system turns sunlight into electricity for a home or a small shop. It has five main parts. The solar panel makes electricity from sunlight during the day. The charge controller sends that electricity safely into the battery and stops it from overcharging or draining too far. The battery stores energy for the night. The lights and appliances (loads) use the energy. Some systems have an inverter, which changes the battery's DC power into AC power for normal plugs.
Many small kits come as one box with the controller and battery built in, plus DC lights, a phone charging port, and sometimes a DC radio, TV or fan. DC appliances use less energy than AC ones with an inverter, so they make a small system go further.
Fake and poor-quality kits are common. Before you sell or install a kit, check whether it is certified by VeraSol, an independent quality programme that grew out of Lighting Global. Its free online database (data.verasol.org) lists certified solar energy kits. A certified kit has been tested for its real performance, durability and honest claims. If a kit is not listed, ask for its warranty in writing and test results.
Example: Fatou in Kaolack, Senegal, compares two kits of the same size. One is in the VeraSol database with a written warranty; the other has no label and no warranty. She chooses the certified kit for her customers.
Words to know:
- Solar panel: a flat panel that makes electricity from sunlight.
- Charge controller: a small box that charges the battery safely and protects it.
- Inverter: a device that changes DC battery power into AC power for normal plugs.
- DC and AC: DC is the steady power from batteries and panels; AC is the power from the grid and most normal plugs.
Official sources:
- VeraSol: independent quality assurance for off-grid solar (successor of Lighting Global Quality Assurance)
- VeraSol product database: search certified solar energy kits
Try it now: Look at a solar kit (in a shop, at home, or a picture online) and write the name of each part. If you have data, search for one kit in the VeraSol database and write whether it is listed.
You can now name each part of a solar home system and check whether a kit is certified.

check.q: Which part stops the battery from overcharging?
check.why: The charge controller charges the battery safely and protects it from overcharging and over-draining.

check.q: Where can you check whether a solar kit is certified?
check.why: VeraSol's free database lists independently tested and certified kits.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Sizing a system from what a household uses
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Calculate a household's daily energy need and choose a panel and battery size.
This lesson builds toward: Given a list of what a household wants to power, you will calculate the daily energy need in watt-hours and choose a panel and battery size, with the arithmetic correct and an allowance for losses.
Size a system from what the family really wants to power. For each item, multiply its power in watts (W) by the hours it is used each day. That gives watt-hours (Wh) per day. Add them up.
Example (figures are examples only): 3 LED bulbs of 3 W for 5 hours = 45 Wh. Charging 2 phones, about 10 Wh each = 20 Wh. A radio, 5 W for 4 hours = 20 Wh. A DC TV, 20 W for 3 hours = 60 Wh. Total: 145 Wh per day. Add about 30% for losses in wires, the controller and the battery: about 190 Wh per day.
Panel: divide the daily need by the peak sun hours where the customer lives (the hours of full-strength sun in a day). If there are about 5 peak sun hours: 190 / 5 = 38 W. Round up to the next panel size, for example a 50 W panel. Peak sun hours change with place and season; check local data or ask an experienced installer, and size for the cloudiest months.
Battery: it must hold at least one night's need. Most batteries should not be emptied fully. A lithium battery is often used to about 80%; a lead-acid one to about 50% (check the maker's figure). For 190 Wh with lithium: 190 / 0.8 = about 238 Wh. For a 12 V battery, divide by 12: about 20 Ah. Add more if the family wants power on cloudy days.
Step by step:
- List each item, its watts and its hours per day.
- Multiply watts by hours for each, and add: Wh per day.
- Add about 30% for losses.
- Panel: daily need / peak sun hours, then round up.
- Battery: daily need / usable share (for example 0.8), then / 12 for amp-hours at 12 V.
Words to know:
- Watt (W): how much power an item uses at one moment.
- Watt-hour (Wh): energy used: watts multiplied by hours.
- Peak sun hours: the number of hours of full-strength sun in a day at a place.
- Amp-hour (Ah): how much charge a battery holds; Wh = Ah x volts.
Try it now: Make an energy table for your own home or a neighbour's: each item, watts, hours, Wh. Add the total, add 30%, and work out the panel and battery size using the steps.
You can now work out a household's daily energy need and choose a panel and battery size for it.

check.q: A 4 W bulb is used for 6 hours a day. How many watt-hours is that?
A household needs 200 Wh a day and there are 5 peak sun hours. What is the smallest panel size from the sum?
check.why: 200 / 5 = 40 W; then round up to the next panel size available.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Installing a small system safely
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Install a small DC solar home system following a safety checklist.
This lesson builds toward: When installing a small DC solar home system, you will follow a safety checklist for panel placement, wiring, fuses and battery placement, with no step missed and no work on the grid or mains wiring.
Panel: put it where it gets full sun most of the day, with no shade from trees, walls or wires. Point it towards the equator: in countries north of the equator, face it south; south of the equator, face it north. Tilt it at least a little, so rain washes off dust. Fix it firmly so wind cannot lift it. On a roof, use a safe ladder, have a helper hold it, and never work in rain or wind.
Battery: keep it indoors, in a dry, shaded and ventilated place, off the floor and out of children's reach, away from cooking fires. Lead-acid batteries give off flammable gas when charging and contain acid: ventilate them, wear eye protection and gloves, and keep flames away. A short circuit across a battery's terminals can melt wires and start a fire.
Wiring: use the cable size the kit maker gives, keep red to positive (+) and black to negative (-), and fit the fuse or breaker the maker gives, close to the battery. For most kits with a separate controller, connect the battery to the controller first, then the panel, then the loads; follow the maker's manual if it says otherwise. Secure cables so they cannot be pulled or chewed.
Limits: this course covers small DC systems only. Never connect a solar system to the grid or to the house's mains wiring, and never open an inverter. Those jobs need a licensed electrician. Some countries license solar technicians; in Kenya, check with EPRA, and elsewhere with your energy regulator.
Step by step:
- Choose a sunny, shade-free spot; face the panel towards the equator with a small tilt; fix it firmly.
- Work at height only with a safe ladder and a helper; never in rain or wind.
- Place the battery indoors: dry, shaded, ventilated, off the floor, away from children and fire.
- Use the right cable, red to +, black to -, and fit the fuse near the battery.
- Connect battery to controller first, then panel, then loads, unless the manual says otherwise.
- No grid or mains connection; no opening the inverter.
Words to know:
- Polarity: which wire is positive (+) and which is negative (-). Getting it wrong can damage parts.
- Fuse: a small safety part that breaks the circuit if too much current flows.
- Ventilated: with fresh air moving through, so gases do not build up.
Official sources:
- Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority (EPRA), Kenya: renewable energy and licensing
- NFPA: Lithium-ion battery safety (warning signs; do not put in the trash, recycle)
Try it now: Write your installation safety checklist with at least eight lines from this lesson. If you can, walk around a home and choose the best place for the panel and the battery, and write why.
You can now install a small DC solar home system safely, following a checklist, and know which jobs to leave to a licensed electrician.

check.q: A customer's home is in Nairobi, just south of the equator. Which way should the panel face?
check.why: Panels face the equator; south of it, that means facing north.

check.q: A customer asks you to connect his solar kit to the grid wiring in his house. What do you do?
options: Refuse: grid and mains work needs a licensed electrician
check.why: This course covers small DC systems only; grid and mains work need a licensed electrician.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: Keeping it working and running a solar business

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Maintenance and finding simple faults
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Carry out routine maintenance and find simple faults step by step.
This lesson builds toward: When a system is not working well, you will carry out routine maintenance and find simple faults step by step, checking the panel, connections, controller and battery in order.
A well-kept system lasts for years. Teach the customer: clean the panel with water and a soft cloth when it is dusty, early in the morning or evening when it is cool (never with soap that leaves a film, and never stand on it). Cut back new shade from trees. Keep the battery clean and dry. Switch off loads that are not needed.
When a customer says "the lights die early", check in order: (1) Panel: is it dirty or shaded now? (2) Connections: any loose, broken or corroded wires or plugs? (3) Controller: what do its lights or screen show? Read the manual for what they mean. (4) Battery: is it old, swollen, hot or leaking? (5) Loads: has the family added a bigger TV or more bulbs than the system was sized for?
Many faults are dirt, shade, loose plugs or extra loads. A swollen, very hot or leaking battery must be replaced; never charge or open it. Old batteries are e-waste: never burn, bury or dump them, and give them to an approved collector or the kit company's take-back scheme.
Example: Chinedu in Kano gets a call that lights die by 8 pm. He finds a new tree branch shading the panel and a second TV added. He cuts the branch with the owner's permission and explains the system's size; the family decides to add a second panel.
Step by step:
- Check the panel: clean and unshaded?
- Check connections: loose, broken or corroded?
- Check the controller lights or screen against the manual.
- Check the battery: old, swollen, hot or leaking?
- Check the loads: more or bigger items than planned?
Words to know:
- Corrosion: green or white crust on metal connections that stops power flowing well.
- Take-back scheme: a company's programme to collect its old products for safe recycling.
Official sources:
- NFPA: Lithium-ion battery safety (warning signs; do not put in the trash, recycle)
- WHO fact sheet: Electronic waste (e-waste), including the dangers of burning and dumping
Try it now: Write a maintenance card for a customer (four lines of routine care) and a five-step fault-finding list you will carry to every call-out.
You can now teach a customer how to look after their system and find simple faults in the right order.

check.q: Lights die early. What is the first thing to check?
options: Whether the panel is dirty or shaded
check.why: Start with the panel: dirt and new shade are common, easy causes.

check.q: You find a battery that is swollen and hot. What do you do?
options: Replace it; do not charge or open it
check.why: A swollen, hot battery is dangerous and must be replaced safely.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Selling honestly: cash and pay-as-you-go
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Explain the cash price and pay-as-you-go terms so a customer can say the total they will pay.
This lesson builds toward: When you sell a system to a customer, you will write an honest quote with the cash price, any pay-as-you-go terms, the total cost and the warranty, so the customer can say the total they will pay before signing.
Many families cannot pay the full price at once, so many companies sell kits on pay-as-you-go (PAYGo). The customer pays a deposit, then small payments, often daily, weekly or monthly by mobile money. If payments stop, the kit locks until they pay again. After the last payment, the customer owns it.
PAYGo helps families get solar sooner, but the total is usually more than the cash price. An honest seller shows both. Example (figures are examples only): cash price KES 20,000. PAYGo: deposit KES 2,000, then KES 1,500 a month for 18 months: 2,000 + (1,500 x 18) = KES 29,000 in total. The customer should be able to say that total before signing.
GOGLA, the off-grid solar industry association, has a consumer protection code built on responsible sales and pricing (do not sell more than the family can afford), transparency (clear, honest information), fair and respectful treatment, good service and product quality. Follow it whether or not your company has signed.
Never promise more than the system can power. Never ask a customer for their mobile money PIN; payments go to the company's official number or till, and a real company never asks for a PIN.
Step by step:
- Show the cash price.
- Show the PAYGo deposit, payment size, how often and for how long.
- Work out the total PAYGo cost with the customer.
- Explain what happens if a payment is missed, and the warranty.
- Check the customer can afford the payments; never ask for a PIN.
Words to know:
- PAYGo (pay-as-you-go): buying a kit with a deposit and small payments; it locks if payments stop and is yours after the last one.
- Deposit: the first payment before the customer takes the kit.
- Consumer protection: rules and habits that treat customers fairly and honestly.
Official sources:
- GOGLA: Consumer protection in off-grid solar (responsible sales, transparency, fair treatment, good service, quality)
Try it now: For a kit you know (or the example), write the cash price and PAYGo terms side by side, and work out the total PAYGo cost. Practise explaining it out loud in under one minute.
You can now explain cash and pay-as-you-go prices honestly so a customer knows the total before signing.

check.q: PAYGo deposit XOF 10,000, then XOF 5,000 a month for 12 months. What is the total?

options: Promising the kit will run a fridge when it cannot
Showing the cash price and the total PAYGo cost side by side
Selling a family more than they can pay
check.why: Transparency means showing both prices clearly.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a quote and running your solar business
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a complete, honest quote for one household.
This lesson builds toward: When you sell a system to a customer, you will write an honest quote with the cash price, any pay-as-you-go terms, the total cost and the warranty, so the customer can say the total they will pay before signing. Given a list of what a household wants to power, you will calculate the daily energy need in watt-hours and choose a panel and battery size, with the arithmetic correct and an allowance for losses.
A good quote wins trust. It shows the customer what they asked to power, the energy table, the system you chose and why, the price, the payment terms and the warranty. It also has your name and phone number, and the date.
Your own price for an installation must cover the kit, cables and fittings, transport to the home, your time, and a profit. Example (figures are examples only): kit MAD 2,500, cables and fittings MAD 300, transport MAD 150, labour MAD 400: cost MAD 3,350. Add MAD 400 profit: MAD 3,750.
After the installation, give the customer a card: maintenance steps, what the controller lights mean, the warranty, and your number for problems. Come back after one month to check. Happy customers send neighbours; that is how solar businesses grow in villages from Kitui to Kaolack.
Keep a simple record of each job: the customer, the kit and its serial number, the date, the price and any call-backs. It helps you honour warranties and see which kits fail.
Step by step:
- Write the energy table and the sizing you did.
- Name the kit, and whether it is certified or has a written warranty.
- Add your safety checklist.
- Show the cash price and any PAYGo terms with the total.
- Attach the maintenance and warranty card, with your name, number and the date.
Words to know:
- Quote: a written offer that shows what you will supply and do, and the price.
- Serial number: the unique number on a product, used for its warranty.
- Call-back: a return visit to fix a problem after the installation.
Try it now: Write your full quote for one household, as described in the final task. Read it to a friend and ask them to tell you the total they would pay.
You can now write a complete, honest quote for a solar home system and keep good records of every job.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Quality checked The kit is not named, or quality is not checked. The kit and its parts are named, and the quote records whether it is in the VeraSol database or has a written warranty. It also explains to the customer why a certified kit matters. Sized correctly No energy table, or the arithmetic is wrong. The energy table, the 30% allowance, and the panel and battery sizes are worked out correctly. It also allows for cloudy days or the cloudiest months, and says where the sun-hours figure came from. Safe installation No checklist, or it includes grid or mains work. The checklist covers panel placement, ladder safety, battery placement, polarity, fuse and connection order, with no grid work. It also names the energy regulator to check for licensing. Care and faults No maintenance card, or unsafe advice. The card gives routine care and the five-step fault order, and says how old batteries are handled. It also explains the controller's lights for this kit. Honest price and terms The total PAYGo cost or the warranty is missing, or the arithmetic is wrong. The cash price, any PAYGo terms and the correct total are shown side by side, with the warranty and the installer's contact. It also checks that the payments fit the family's budget and says what happens if a payment is missed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part of your quote and try again.

check.q: Which item belongs on every quote?
options: The total the customer will pay, and the warranty
A promise of free power forever
check.why: The total cost and warranty let the customer decide fairly.

check.q: Why put the energy table on the quote?
options: It shows how you sized the system to the family's real use
check.why: The table shows the system matches what the family will power.
